subject: geography

moments.title: Burgess's concentric zone model
moments.body: Burgess publishes 'The Growth of the City' as part of the Chicago School volume. He describes a model of concentric zones radiating from the central business district: factory zone, zone of transition (worst housing, immigrants), workers' homes, residential, commuter zone.
moments.takeaway: The model was based on 1920s Chicago — a specific city in a specific moment. Generalising it has caused decades of misapplication.

moments.title: Hoyt's sector model
moments.body: Hoyt's 'The Structure and Growth of Residential Neighborhoods in American Cities' argues land use grows in sectors along transport corridors, not concentric rings. High-income areas tend to expand outward along a single axis.
moments.takeaway: By the late 1930s, alternative urban models were already correcting Burgess. The discipline has produced many more since (Harris and Ullman's multiple-nuclei model, 1945; postmodern Los Angeles School).

now.title: Models with limits
now.body: The Chicago School urban models remain standard textbook material despite being based on early 20th-century American industrial cities. They struggle with megacities of the Global South, polycentric urban regions and gated communities. The 'Los Angeles School' (Ed Soja, Michael Dear) argues for a different model with no clear centre.
now.open_questions: Should generic urban models be taught at all? Models are simplified abstractions; their value depends on whether they describe the cities the student will encounter.

reflection: Disciplinary classics get taught long after their empirical basis has shifted. Burgess's Chicago rings sit in geography textbooks 100 years later — useful for teaching the idea of urban structure, dangerous if treated as a description of all cities.
